overview: Xhosa-speaking societies of South Africa’s Eastern Cape combined farming, cattle keeping, craftsmanship and rich oral and written traditions. Their rulers and communities faced repeated colonial wars and dispossession. The map’s broad label covers several political communities, whose alliances and experiences were not identical.

periods.title: Frontier wars and dispossession
periods.summary: Repeated conflicts over land, cattle and authority expanded colonial control in the Eastern Cape.

periods.title: A catastrophic cattle-killing movement
periods.summary: Prophecy amid disease and colonial pressure led many people to destroy cattle and crops, with devastating consequences.

periods.title: Further conquest and resistance
periods.summary: The final frontier war of 1877 to 1878 brought renewed dispossession and defeat.

items.text: After the famine associated with the 1856 to 1857 cattle-killing, thousands of Xhosa people were moved into the Cape Colony as laborers. Colonial occupation also removed land from Gcaleka ruler Sarhili. The disaster reshaped households as well as boundaries.

Alliances divided communities. During the 1877 to 1878 war, Sandile led some Rharhabe into resistance while others remained aligned with the Cape government. Mfengu forces were major colonial allies. This was a struggle involving African political choices alongside imperial power.

Peires links the 1856 to 1857 cattle-killing beliefs to the deadly cattle lungsickness epidemic that began in 1854, together with indigenous and Christian ideas of renewal. Understanding that setting helps explain people’s hopes without treating the prophecy as true or the victims as a joke.

A museum study records Xhosa milk vessels made from soft woods, alongside evidence of earlier basket containers. The materials changed, but the practical problem remained the same: carrying and storing a food central to cattle-keeping households.

A Xhosa necklace collected around 1877, South African Museum object SAM-10920, uses small pieces of fragrant tambuti wood. Jewelry could appeal to the nose as well as the eye. The surviving object makes a personal fashion choice tangible.

The ugwali instrument combined a wooden or reed stave, a sinew string and a flattened feather quill. Early nineteenth-century writers recorded it among Xhosa musicians. A modest handful of materials could become an instrument with a distinctive sound.

Xhosa pipe makers lined wooden bowls with sheet metal to protect the wood from burning. Museum examples even preserve printing on recycled tin. The object shows careful fitting, material knowledge and reuse.

Craft workers drilled narrow channels through wooden pipe stems and closed unwanted drill exits with closely fitted wooden plugs. Later souvenir production adapted these skills to visitors’ tastes. The finished smooth surface could conceal several stages of painstaking work.

sections.title: Print, education and a later childhood

items.text: “Indaba” means “News.” It was the title of a Xhosa-language monthly published at Lovedale from 1862 to 1865. Its title offers a small sample of written Xhosa from the map’s own nineteenth-century period.

Despite missionary editorial restrictions, writers including John Muir Vimbe, William Kobe Ntsikana and Tiyo Soga contributed to Indaba. Soga’s translation of the first part of The Pilgrim’s Progress appeared in 1867. Xhosa authors used print to build a literary public.

The literary story continued after 1878. As editor of Isigidimi in the 1880s, W. W. Gqoba published poetry that challenged missionary education. Schools and newspapers offered opportunities, but African writers also questioned the inequalities within them.

For a later glimpse of a related Xhosa-speaking community, Nelson Mandela remembered his Thembu childhood at Qunu in the 1920s: children shaped clay oxen, wagons and birds, and slid down a sloping rock on flat stones. His memoir gives us a named childhood, not a universal custom.

ending.text: Sandile died during the 1878 war, and colonial expansion continued afterward. Political defeat did not end Xhosa communities, language or literature; the imported endpoint marks a colonial conflict, not a people’s disappearance.
